newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori strongly denies Peru may free rebels.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori strongly denies Peru may free rebels.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori vehemently denied on Thursday his government would free jailed Marxist rebels in a deal to end the 93-day hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's Lima home.

"I absolutely, totally and flatly deny that my government's position has changed," said Fujimori, referring to reports he might be willing to free some Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) detainees in order to end the hostage standoff.
"My government's position remains the same. There will be no freeing of MRTA prisoners," Fujimori said on local broadcaster Radioprogramas del Peru in an interview from the central Andes.

He was responding to media speculation that he may have agreed at a meeting this week with Japan's Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura to free MRTA detainees to secure the release of 72 dignitaries being held by about 20 MRTA rebels.

MRTA has demanded release of 450 of its Marxist comrades from jail in exchange for release of the hostages, held in the Japanese residence since Dec. 17. Fujimori has consistently rejected the demand but signalled he may be flexible in other areas.
"The security of the country comes before any other interest. I'm sorry if that sounds hard," said Fujimori, in his first statements about the crisis since Komura's visit.

He said the liberation of MRTA prisoners would set a dangerous precedent for a country that had suffered violence since 1980 in wars launched by the MRTA and larger Maoist Shining Path guerrilla group.
"We cannot backslide here because this may generate other cases in which I am asked to free prisoners, including other terrorist groups or common criminals," he added.
Cuba confirmed on Thursday it had accepted a formal request from Japan to grant asylum to the hostage-takers if it would contribute to ending the crisis and if all sides agreed to the arrangement.
Guerrilla-related violence has cost Peru 30,000 lives and close to $25 billion in infrastructure damage in 17 years.
Fujimori spoke from Picoy in the Andes above Lima, a town that "has suffered the waves of terrorism and where there have been so many victims."

He said his government would continue searching for a peaceful end to the crisis and that discussions on Tuesday with Komura had served to better coordinate efforts to find asylum for the rebels in another country.
The MRTA rebels have said they will not back down on their main demand of freedom for some 460 jailed comrades and have said they do not want to leave Peru.
They initially took hundreds of hostages when they stormed the residence in Lima's San Isidro neighbourhood but released in the following days all but their most prized bargaining chips.
Among the captives are Fujimori's brother Pedro, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
